title: Kickstarter a decade after Mollick (2014): failures still fail badly, while successes now overshoot their goals
abstract: We replicate the findings of Mollick (2014) on Kickstarter success that public data allow us to test, using every available monthly scrape published by Web Robots from 2014 to 2026, deduplicated to 643,007 projects. The hypotheses, sample rules and decision criteria were pre-registered and committed before any data were downloaded, and every departure from the plan is recorded with its reason; the main sample comprises 357,835 completed US projects with goals from US$100 to US$1,000,000, as in the original. Descriptive findings are judged against a pre-set smallest difference of interest (5 percentage points for shares, 0.05 for funding ratios), and regression findings by direction and confidence interval. Failures still fail by large margins and smaller failures by smaller ones, and larger goals and longer campaigns still reduce the odds of success while being a staff pick raises them; the regression findings hold in 18 of 18 launch years taken separately for goal size, 18 of 18 for duration and 18 of 18 for staff picks, and the failure margins meet the pre-set criteria in 16 of 18. The exception is the narrowness of success: far more successful projects now raise several times their goal, so that finding holds as a pattern but has changed over time. The conclusions hold when cancelled projects are counted as failures, when all countries are included, when goal limits are varied or adjusted for inflation, and in 125 of 127 individual scrapes for the goal effect. Limitations: the data are scraped, not supplied by Kickstarter; 55% of projects in the sample succeeded, above Kickstarter's reported overall rate, which suggests over-representation of successful older projects, although the regression findings also hold in 2009 to 2013, when coverage was essentially complete; the staff-pick field may not match Mollick's featuring measure; the video test is exploratory and limited to 2024 to 2026; and the associations are not causal. Code, pre-registration, deviations and results are at the artefact link.

claims.text: Among 195,534 successful US Kickstarter projects launched 2009 to 2026, 29.2% [29.0%, 29.4%] raised at least twice their goal, against about one in nine (11.1%) reported by Mollick (2014) for 2009 to 2012.

The median successful project raised 1.264 times its goal [1.261, 1.267] and the lower quartile 1.065, against Mollick's 1.10 and 1.03; successes still cluster near their goals, but less narrowly than in 2009 to 2012.
Failed projects (n = 162,301) raised a mean 0.097 of their goal [0.097, 0.098]; 10.8% reached 30% and 3.9% reached half, against Mollick's 0.103, 10% and 3%, so failures still fail by large margins.
Failed projects with goals under US$1,000 raised a mean 0.150 of their goal and those over US$1,000 a mean 0.091 (difference 0.059, 95% CI [0.056, 0.062]), replicating Mollick's 0.147 and 0.098.
In a logistic regression on 193,050 projects with goals of US$5,000 or more, the odds ratio for log goal is 0.553 [0.547, 0.560], below one in 18 of 18 launch years and weaker than Mollick's 0.23.
In the same regression each additional day of campaign duration has an odds ratio of 0.977 [0.976, 0.978], below one in 18 of 18 launch years, consistent with Mollick's 0.99.
Being a Kickstarter staff pick has an odds ratio for success of 19.55 [18.75, 20.38], above one in 18 of 18 launch years, against the 20.47 Mollick reported for featuring on the home page.

Exploratory, decided after data access: among 17,296 projects launched 2024 to 2026 with goals of US$5,000 or more, having a video has an odds ratio for success of 2.07 [1.88, 2.27], against Mollick's 4.3.
